purpose: Catches structural decisions — macro placement, aspect ratio, power grid pitch, I/O ring, hard-block orientation — that determine whether placement can be legal, routable, and timing-convergent. These cannot be cheaply undone after placement or CTS; a bad floorplan guarantees congestion and IR-drop failures downstream.

checks.question: What is the core utilization target and does the placement-blockage/halo strategy support it across the die?
checks.evidence_demanded: Floorplan utilization report + cell-density map; macro halo/channel measurements; utilization histogram by region
checks.red_flag: Overall utilization > 70% with one or more regions already > 80%, or macro channels < 3–5 µm — congestion is structurally baked in
checks.why_it_matters: A floorplan that exceeds ~70–75% utilization leaves no slack for placement optimization; downstream placement will be unroutable and pre-CTS timing will be dominated by wire delay.

checks.question: Are hard macros placed to minimize long global nets and to open routing channels, and are their pins facing the core?
checks.evidence_demanded: Floorplan GDS overlay with macro placement; pin-access direction annotation; global-route congestion map (early trial route)
checks.red_flag: Macros hugging the die center, pin orientations facing away from the core, or macro edges aligned to create narrow channels — early global route shows overflow > 0 in those channels
checks.why_it_matters: Macro placement drives both congestion and timing. A macro channel that is too narrow cannot be routed at advanced nodes (≤7nm) where pin-access is the dominant congestion source; at 28nm the same channel might barely route but with severe timing penalty.

checks.question: Does the power grid (rings, straps, rails) meet IR-drop and EM budgets before any cells are placed?
checks.evidence_demanded: Early power-grid IR-drop analysis (static) with strap width/pitch; EM check on power routes; PG connectivity report
checks.red_flag: Static IR drop > 5% Vdd at 28nm (or > 3% at ≤7nm), or any strap segment exceeding EM current-density limits — grid must be revised now
checks.why_it_matters: Power grid weakness is the #1 cause of late-stage, expensive re-route. At ≤7nm, metal resistance is ~10× that of 28nm, so a grid that was adequate at 28nm will fail IR at 7nm; the grid pitch/width decision is made here and cannot be changed after placement.

checks.question: Are I/O pads placed to match the package bond/ball map, with clock pins separated from analog/noisy signals?
checks.evidence_demanded: I/O placement vs. package pin-out diagram; signal-integrity annotation (clock vs. analog proximity)
checks.red_flag: I/O order does not match package pin-out, or clock I/O adjacent to analog I/O without guard rings — package will mis-wire or suffer crosstalk
checks.why_it_matters: I/O-to-package mismatch is a tape-out-killing error that cannot be detected by any EDA check; it is caught only by human review against the package drawing. Clock-adjacent analog I/O causes SI failures that surface only in silicon.

checks.question: Is the die aspect ratio compatible with the package and manufacturing reticle limit, with scribe lines and dicing streets reserved?
checks.evidence_demanded: Die dimensions vs. reticle limit; scribe-line width confirmation from fab/OSAT; multi-project-wafer (MPW) street reservation
checks.red_flag: Aspect ratio > 1.5:1 without justification, or scribe line < 80 µm (consult OSAT) — die cannot be diced or fails reticle limit
checks.why_it_matters: Reticle-limited die must be rejected by the foundry; insufficient scribe lines cause mechanical die damage during singulation. Both are discovered too late if not reviewed here.

checks.question: Are tap cells, tie cells, and well-connectivity correctly planned for the technology (especially multi-well, mixed-signal)?
checks.evidence_demanded: Tap/tie cell insertion plan; well-connectivity report; mixed-signal well-isolation annotation
checks.red_flag: Missing tap cells in high-density regions, tie-high/tie-low cells unconnected, or n-wells of different potential not separated in mixed-signal regions
checks.why_it_matters: Tap cells maintain substrate bias; omitted taps cause latch-up or functional failure. Mixed-signal well isolation errors cause crosstalk and leakage that no timing check catches.

checks.question: Are all hard IP blocks oriented for optimal pin access and signal flow, and do their halos accommodate routing and PG?
checks.evidence_demanded: IP block floorplan with halo dimensions; IP pin list vs. core direction; PG ring around IP
checks.red_flag: IP block rotated arbitrarily so pins face macro edges, or halo < 2 µm preventing rail connection — early route shows 100% overflow at IP boundary
checks.why_it_matters: IP pin orientation determines whether signals can reach the core without detours. At ≤7nm, a mis-oriented IP can make an entire block unroutable. PG halo insufficiency causes IR-drop hotspots at IP boundaries.

checks.question: Is the clock root location and top-level clock distribution strategy consistent with the floorplan geometry?
checks.evidence_demanded: Clock root pin location; planned clock trunk routes; macro placement relative to clock root
checks.red_flag: Clock root at a die corner while the largest clock sink cluster is at the opposite corner, or clock trunks forced through macro channels — predicted insertion delay > target
checks.why_it_matters: CTS quality is largely determined by clock-root-to-sink geometry. A root placement that forces long clock routes will produce high latency and skew that CTS cannot recover, surfacing as a CTS failure gate.

checks.question: Has the aspect ratio and core/site-row plan been validated against the standard-cell library row height and MCMM scenario count?
checks.evidence_demanded: Site row definition; library row-height compatibility; scenario count vs. available optimization resource
checks.red_flag: Row height incompatible with library, or core shape forces excessive row fragmentation — placement legality check fails
checks.why_it_matters: A fragmented core with illegal sites prevents placement legalization; the entire downstream flow stalls. This is a trivial-to-catch, devastating-to-miss error.

kill_questions: Show me the early global-route congestion map — is overflow zero everywhere outside macro channels?
Show me the static IR-drop map — is the worst-case drop within budget for this node?
waiver_culture: In real projects, teams routinely waive the 'perfect' utilization target (accepting 75% instead of 70%) and wave through slightly narrow macro channels on the bet that placement spreading will fix it — the waiver later costs 2–3 weeks of placement iteration, and at ≤7nm often forces a floorplan revision that moves the schedule by a month.

purpose: Validates that placement has produced a structure that CTS can balance and that timing is dominated by logic, not wire — catching placement-driven timing failures, congestion that will block routing, and clock-tree feasibility before the expensive CTS step commits buffer trees and clock latency.

checks.question: What is the distribution of setup slack by clock group — is the wall at zero, not a tail at −300 ps?
checks.evidence_demanded: Pre-CTS setup slack histogram by clock domain; WNS/TNS per scenario; report_timing for worst paths
checks.red_flag: Histogram shows a long tail of violations > 200 ps, or WNS worse than −300 ps in any scenario — placement is structurally failing timing
checks.why_it_matters: Pre-CTS timing should be close to clean. A deep negative tail means logic placement is poor; CTS and post-CTS optimization cannot recover more than ~10–15% of slack. If the wall isn't at zero now, it will never reach zero.

checks.question: Is global-route overflow zero across all GCells, and is track utilization < 70% in all regions?
checks.evidence_demanded: Global-route overflow report; congestion map (GCell-level); track utilization heatmap
checks.red_flag: Overflow > 0 in any GCell, or track utilization > 80% in localized regions — detail route will detour and create DRC
checks.why_it_matters: Non-zero overflow at pre-CTS means the design is unroutable. CTS and routing will not fix congestion; the only remedy is placement re-spread or floorplan change, which is exponentially more expensive after CTS.

checks.question: Are design-rule violations (DRV) — max transition, max capacitance, max fanout — within limits across all scenarios?
checks.evidence_demanded: DRV report; worst transition/capacitance/fanout per scenario; cell-level DRV histogram
checks.red_flag: Any DRV violation > 10% over limit, or transition violations on clock-gated paths — CTS will inherit and amplify these
checks.why_it_matters: DRVs are the seed of post-CTS timing failures. A cell with excess capacitance will have slow transition; CTS inserts buffers that cascade the problem. Cleaning DRVs now is 10× cheaper than fixing after CTS.

checks.question: Is placement legality 100% — no overlapping cells, all cells on legal sites, no placement-blockage violations?
checks.evidence_demanded: check_placement legality report; overlap/illegal-site summary
checks.red_flag: Any illegal placement, overlap, or off-site cell — CTS and routing will silently produce geometry errors
checks.why_it_matters: Illegal placement propagates as DRC violations and potential functional errors into GDS. CTS assumes legal placement; an illegal cell may receive no clock or be unroutable.

checks.question: Is the clock-tree structure feasible — are all clock sinks reachable within the target skew and latency budget from the clock root?
checks.evidence_demanded: Early clock-tree estimation report; clock sink clustering; insertion-delay prediction per sink
checks.red_flag: Predicted insertion delay spread > 2× target latency, or any sink cluster > 500 µm from clock root — CTS will not converge to skew target
checks.why_it_matters: CTS cannot recover from a fundamentally unbalanced clock topology. If the root is poorly located or macro placement blocks clock routes, CTS will explode buffer count and still miss skew. This must be caught before CTS runs.

checks.question: Are timing exceptions (false paths, multicycle paths, case-analysis) verified complete and correct?
checks.evidence_demanded: check_timing report; SDC exception list cross-referenced with RTL intent; CDC verification report
checks.red_flag: Unconstrained paths, missing multicycle declarations, or false paths that cover real timing paths — STA numbers are meaningless
checks.why_it_matters: Incorrect exceptions produce either false violations (wasted optimization) or masked real violations (silicon failure). This is the highest-risk area of pre-CTS review; a single missed false-path can hide a critical bug.

checks.question: Is the cell density distribution uniform and are there no localized utilization hotspots > 80%?
checks.evidence_demanded: Cell density map; utilization histogram by region; overflow correlation
checks.red_flag: Any region > 80% utilization while global avg is 60% — that region will be unroutable and timing-congested
checks.why_it_matters: Localized high density is the signature of poor placement spreading. It is the direct cause of both congestion and wire-dominated timing failure. At ≤7nm, a 5% density hotspot can make an entire block unroutable due to pin-access starvation.

checks.question: Are hold-time violations minimal and are they explained by useful-skew headroom rather than structural issues?
checks.evidence_demanded: Pre-CTS hold slack histogram; worst hold violation per scenario; skew-group report
checks.red_flag: Hold violations > 100 ps in functional mode, or hold violations on paths where useful skew could help — indicates placement imbalance
checks.why_it_matters: Pre-CTS hold should be near zero or slightly positive. Large hold violations mean placement is imbalanced; CTS will introduce positive skew that converts these to even larger hold violations. Catching them now allows placement re-optimization; after CTS, the only fix is data-path delay buffers.

checks.question: Is the clock-tree structure feasible — are all clock sinks reachable within the target skew and latency budget from the clock root?
checks.evidence_demanded: Early clock-tree estimation report; clock sink clustering; insertion-delay prediction per sink
checks.red_flag: Predicted insertion delay spread > 2× target latency, or any sink cluster > 500 µm from clock root — CTS will not converge to skew target
checks.why_it_matters: CTS cannot recover from a fundamentally unbalanced clock topology. If the root is poorly located or macro placement blocks clock routes, CTS will explode buffer count and still miss skew. This must be caught before CTS runs.

kill_questions: Show me the pre-CTS setup slack histogram by clock group — is the wall at zero, not a tail at −300 ps?
Show me the global-route overflow report — is it zero in every GCell?
waiver_culture: Teams commonly waive minor DRV violations (>5% over limit) on the assumption that CTS and post-CTS optimization will absorb them — the waiver later costs 1–2 weeks of ECO iterations, and at ≤7nm often forces a floorplan revision that moves the schedule by a month.

purpose: The final gate before GDS is frozen — verifies that timing is closed across all process/voltage/temperature corners, all modes (functional, scan, etc.), and all scenarios, with proper OCV/AOCV/POCV derating, SI-aware analysis, and realistic parasitics. This is the last point where a timing escape can be caught without a respin.

checks.question: Is timing closed across ALL required corners and scenarios simultaneously — not just the nominal worst case?
checks.evidence_demanded: MCMM STA report: setup/hold WNS/TNS per corner × mode; PBA timing on worst paths; OCV/AOCV/POCV derating report
checks.red_flag: Any negative slack in any corner/mode combination, or a corner that was not analyzed because 'it never fails' — the chip will fail in silicon at that corner
checks.why_it_matters: Partial-corner signoff is the #1 cause of chips that pass STA but fail in the field. At ≤7nm, variation is high enough that the worst corner can shift between SS/FF depending on the path; skipping any corner is gambling the entire tapeout.

checks.question: Are parasitics extracted with the signoff RC engine (not the trial-route estimate), and is the RC correlation error < 5%?
checks.evidence_demanded: StarRC/Calibre xACT extraction vs. Innov/ICC2 trial-route RC correlation report; post-route vs. signoff parasitic timing delta
checks.red_flag: Correlation error > 5%, or signoff uses trial-route RC — the timing numbers are optimistic by 5–10%
checks.why_it_matters: Trial-route RC is an estimate. If the correlation is poor, the design 'meets timing' in implementation but fails in signoff. This gap is discovered only at the signoff gate, forcing ECOs that can invalidate the entire timing closure.

checks.question: Is OCV/AOCV/POCV derating applied appropriately for the node, and is the derating depth sufficient?
checks.evidence_demanded: Derating report; LVF-based POCV coefficient files; comparison of flat OCV vs. AOCV vs. POCV slack impact
checks.red_flag: At ≤7nm using flat OCV instead of POCV, or derating depth < 2 levels — the analysis is either too optimistic or pessimistically over-constraining
checks.why_it_matters: Flat OCV at advanced nodes is dangerously optimistic — it hides variation-induced failures. Conversely, AOCV without proper coefficient calibration over-constrains, wasting power/area. The choice directly affects yield.

checks.question: Are all timing exceptions (false path, multicycle, case-analysis) verified against RTL and CDC analysis?
checks.evidence_demanded: SDC exception audit; CDC verification report; formal check that false/multicycle paths match RTL intent
checks.red_flag: Any false path that covers a real functional path, or any multicycle missing its -hold counterpart — STA is silently lying
checks.why_it_matters: A wrong exception masks a real violation. The chip passes STA but fails intermittently in silicon. This is the most insidious class of timing escape because it is invisible to all standard checks.

checks.question: Is setup and hold timing closed WITH realistic clock uncertainty — including jitter, MMMS skew estimate accuracy, and any guardband?
checks.evidence_demanded: Clock uncertainty breakdown (jitter + estimated skew + guardband); pre-CTS vs. post-CTS uncertainty reconciliation; final signoff uncertainty value
checks.red_flag: Uncertainty reduced to jitter-only with zero guardband, or uncertainty still contains pre-CTS skew estimate (over-pessimistic) — either over- or under-margin
checks.why_it_matters: Zero guardband at signoff means the chip has no margin against process variation → systematic yield loss. Over-pessimistic uncertainty means the chip could have run faster — performance left on the table. The balance is the crux of signoff.

checks.question: Are the worst setup/hold paths physically plausible — i.e., not the result of pathological corner interaction or parasitic extraction artifact?
checks.evidence_demanded: report_timing -pba_mode path on the top 20 worst paths; physical cross-probe of each; parasitic annotation
checks.red_flag: Worst paths are all in a single improbable corner/mode combination, or all involve a single net with anomalous parasitic values — likely an artifact, not a real problem
checks.why_it_matters: Chasing artifact violations wastes ECO effort and can destabilize the design. Conversely, dismissing 'artifact' violations without proof risks shipping a real bug. The reviewer must physically cross-probe each worst path.

checks.question: Is there sufficient timing margin for aging (NBTI/PBTI) and supply noise at the target lifetime?
checks.evidence_demanded: Aging analysis report (NBTI/PBTI); supply-noise-induced timing degradation estimate; margin budget vs. required product lifetime
checks.red_flag: No aging analysis performed, or margin < 5% of cycle time at end-of-life — the chip will fail after 1–2 years in the field
checks.why_it_matters: Aging is a slow, systematic failure mechanism. At ≤7nm, NBTI/PBTI degradation is significant. Shipping without aging margin means field returns 18–24 months post-tapeout — the most expensive failure mode possible.

checks.question: Are all clock-domain-crossing paths properly constrained (false-path or bounded max/min delay), and is the MTBF of each synchronizer acceptable?
checks.evidence_demanded: CDC constraint audit; MTBF report per synchronizer based on failure rate; max/min delay values vs. synchronizer structure
checks.red_flag: CDC paths timed as single-cycle, or false-pathed without MTBF justification — either massive spurious violations or hidden metastability risk
checks.why_it_matters: Mis-constrained CDC is a classic source of chips that 'work on the bench but fail in the field'. The MTBF calculation is the only objective measure; without it, the team is guessing.

checks.question: Is the timing ECO minimal and has it not destabilized other paths — i.e., is the final state a true global optimum, not a whack-a-mole patch?
checks.evidence_demanded: ECO history; incremental STA after each ECO; overall WNS/TNS trend; comparison of pre-ECO vs. post-ECO timing across all scenarios
checks.red_flag: ECOs are still in progress at signoff, or each ECO fixes one path while degrading 2 others (negative TNS trend) — the design is not converged
checks.why_it_matters: Whack-a-mole ECOs indicate the design is not at a stable optimum. The last ECO before tapeout can inadvertently break a path that was previously clean. The reviewer must see a convergent ECO history, not an ongoing battle.

kill_questions: Show me the MCMM STA summary — is WNS ≥ 0 in every corner × mode × scenario?
Show me the RC correlation report — is the signoff extraction within 5% of the implementation RC?
waiver_culture: The most common waiver at this gate is accepting a small negative slack (−10 to −30 ps) in a 'never-happens' corner on the reasoning that 'process won't be that slow' — the waiver later costs the entire tapeout when silicon from a slow lot fails in that corner. Another common waiver is skipping POCV in favor of flat OCV to 'save run time', which hides variation-induced escapes.

purpose: The absolute final gate before GDS ships to the foundry — verifies the geometry is manufacturable (DRC), the connectivity matches the netlist (LVS), no plasma damage will occur (antenna), no electrical reliability issues exist (ERC), and all foundry-specific rules (DFM, density, metal fill) are satisfied. Nothing can be fixed after this point without a respin.

checks.question: Is DRC 100% clean with the FOUNDRY's latest rule deck, not the PDK-bundled version?
checks.evidence_demanded: Signoff DRC report (Calibre/ICV) with foundry's current rule deck version; zero violations; waiver log if any
checks.red_flag: Any DRC violation, or the rule deck is the PDK-bundled version rather than the foundry's latest download (65nm and below require the latest DFM-aware deck)
checks.why_it_matters: A single DRC violation can make a chip unmanufacturable. Foundry updates rule decks regularly; using a stale deck means passing 'clean' on rules that have since been tightened — the chip fails at the foundry. This is non-negotiable: DRC must be 100% clean with the current deck.

checks.question: Is LVS clean — does the extracted netlist match the gate-level netlist exactly, with no shorts, opens, or parameter mismatches?
checks.evidence_demanded: LVS report: compared cells, pins, nets; ERC-LVS cross-check; black-box/IP handling verification
checks.red_flag: Any LVS discrepancy, even 'minor' ones like a floating pin or a deleted net — the physical chip does not match the logical design
checks.why_it_matters: LVS mismatch means the silicon will not function as designed. A short or open anywhere in the power/ground or signal network causes functional failure or latch-up. There is no waiver for LVS; it must be 100% clean.

checks.question: Are all antenna-ratio violations fixed, with antenna diodes inserted where needed and the antenna ratio within foundry limits?
checks.evidence_demanded: Antenna report: PAR (physical antenna ratio) per violating net; diode insertion log; final antenna ratio compliance
checks.red_flag: Any net with PAR > foundry limit, or diodes inserted without verifying they don't create new DRC/antenna issues — the gate oxide will be damaged during fabrication
checks.why_it_matters: Antenna effect damages thin gate oxides during plasma processing, causing immediate or latent transistor failure. At ≤7nm, gate oxides are so thin that even small antenna ratios cause yield loss. Diodes must be placed; the fix cannot be waived.

checks.question: Is ERC clean — no floating wells, no power/ground shorts, no ESD protection gaps, current-density within limits?
checks.evidence_demanded: ERC report; well-connectivity check; PG short/open report; ESD clamp verification; current-density check
checks.red_flag: Floating n-well or p-well, PG short, missing ESD clamp on any I/O, or any net exceeding EM current-density — reliability failure guaranteed
checks.why_it_matters: ERC violations cause latch-up, ESD damage, or electromigration failure in the field. A floating well can cause functional failure or increased leakage. ESD gaps cause I/O death during handling. None of these are visible in timing or functional simulation.

checks.question: Is metal fill / dummy metal inserted to meet density rules, and does it not violate minimum spacing or create new DRC?
checks.evidence_demanded: Metal fill report; density map per layer; foundry density rule compliance; post-fill DRC re-run
checks.red_flag: Any layer below minimum density, or metal fill creating spacing violations, or fill pattern causing CMP dishing — the wafer will have planarization defects
checks.why_it_matters: Dummy metal fill is mandatory for CMP uniformity. Insufficient fill causes thickness variation, affecting transistor performance and potentially causing open/short. Over-fill or improperly placed fill creates new DRCs. This must be re-verified after fill insertion.

checks.question: Are all I/O cells the foundry-provided complete versions, not the abstracted place-and-route versions, and is the I/O ring properly closed with pad fillers?
checks.evidence_demanded: GDS diff: the exported I/O cells match foundry's full I/O GDS; pad filler presence; I/O-to-core connectivity
checks.red_flag: Abstracted I/O cells still in the GDS (instead of foundry's full I/O library), missing pad fillers, or I/O ring gap — the chip cannot bond to the package
checks.why_it_matters: The place-and-route tool's I/O abstraction lacks the full foundry I/O structure. Shipping with abstracted I/O means the actual pad geometry is wrong — bonding fails, or the I/O electrically malfunctions. Pad fillers are required to close the I/O ring; without them, the ring is open.

checks.question: Is the GDS clean of LEF abstracted geometry — all standard cells and macros are represented by their real GDS, not LEF abstracts?
checks.evidence_demanded: GDS stream-out log; cell GDS substitution verification; visual inspection of critical cells
checks.red_flag: Any cell still represented by LEF abstract (rectangles instead of real geometry) — DRC/LVS were run on false geometry
checks.why_it_matters: If the GDS contains LEF abstracts instead of real cell GDS, the DRC/LVS that passed were meaningless — the real geometry may have violations. This is a catastrophic error discovered only when the foundry rejects the GDS.

checks.question: Are all foundry-specific rules satisfied — DFM, via-enclosure, notch, jog, end-of-line, and process-antenna for ALL metal layers?
checks.evidence_demanded: Foundry DFM rule-deck execution; via-array rules; end-of-line rules; process-antenna per layer; DFM waiver log
checks.red_flag: Skipping DFM checks because 'they are warnings not errors' — at ≤7nm, DFM rules are manufacturing-critical, not advisory
checks.why_it_matters: DFM rules at advanced nodes directly affect yield. A missing via-enclosure or improper end-of-line termination causes random opens/shorts. Treating DFM as advisory is the fastest path to a low-yield or zero-yield chip.

checks.question: Is the final GDS verified by importing it BACK into the layout tool and re-running DRC/LVS — the 'round-trip' check?
checks.evidence_demanded: Round-trip verification report: GDS → import → DRC → LVS, all clean; comparison with original DB
checks.red_flag: Round-trip not performed, or discrepancies found between original DB and re-imported GDS — the stream-out process corrupted geometry
checks.why_it_matters: GDS stream-out has many opportunities for data corruption (layer mapping errors, unit mismatches, hierarchy flattening bugs). The only way to catch this is to import the GDS back and re-verify. Skipping this check has shipped multiple historically famous 'dead on arrival' chips.

checks.question: Is the die-to-package interface verified — bump/pad coordinates match the package, polarity marks present, and orientation not ambiguous?
checks.evidence_demanded: GDS vs. package drawing overlay; bump/pad coordinate comparison; orientation marker presence; I/O pin-order vs. package
checks.red_flag: Coordinate mismatch > 1 µm, missing orientation marker, or I/O order ambiguous — the die cannot be correctly bonded or packaged
checks.why_it_matters: A 1 µm shift in bump coordinates can cause open bonds. Missing orientation markers lead to die placed upside-down in the package. Ambiguous I/O order causes mis-wiring. These are packaging-killing errors invisible to all EDA checks.

kill_questions: Show me the signoff DRC report with the FOUNDRY's latest rule deck — is it 100% clean?
Show me the round-trip GDS verification — is DRC/LVS clean on the re-imported GDS?
waiver_culture: In real projects, the most common PV waiver is accepting DFM 'warnings' (not hard errors) at advanced nodes on the rationale that 'DFM is yield-tuning, not manufacturing-critical' — this waiver later costs 10–30% yield, turning a profitable chip into a marginal one. Antenna violations are almost never waived (they cause immediate gateoxide failure), but I have seen teams waive ERC 'minor' floating-well warnings that turned into field latch-up returns. The iron law: DRC and LVS are never waived, ever. Any other waiver is a calculated risk documented in the signoff waiver log.
